claims.text: Structural and chemical stability is governed by the degree of atomic disorder within the solid solution.
Atomic disorder influences phase stability at elevated temperatures.
Elevated temperatures increase atomic disorder in the nanoparticles.
Increased atomic disorder enhances phase stability.
Increased atomic disorder increases resistance to segregation or phase separation.
Nanoparticles with higher atomic disorder will retain structural integrity across 473–1923 K.
Nanoparticles with higher atomic disorder will retain chemical stability across 473–1923 K.
Nanoparticles with lower atomic disorder will exhibit phase separation or degradation.
An oxidizing environment may affect nanoparticle stability relative to an inert atmosphere.
The proposed disorder–stability relationship applies to near-equiatomic nanoparticles containing at least five metals.
The proposed relationship does not apply to systems containing fewer metals or significantly different compositions.
The exact relationship between atomic disorder and stability is not fully characterized.
The effect of specific metal combinations on stability is uncertain.

contradictions.description: The predicted outcome says that low-disorder nanoparticles should show greater degradation or phase separation than high-disorder nanoparticles, but the falsification rule incorrectly identifies that same observation as falsifying the hypothesis.
